title: Extractions & oral surgery
blurb: Pre-op safety checks, forceps and elevators, supporting a surgical extraction, post-op instructions and dry socket.
question: A patient is booked to have 46 extracted. As you set up, you notice the radiograph on screen is of the other side. After the extraction, the patient asks why they must bite on gauze and whether they can rinse. Three days later they phone with worsening pain and a bad taste. What do you do at each point?

teach.body: A simple extraction removes a tooth with forceps and elevators. A surgical extraction is needed when a tooth is buried, broken or impacted: the dentist lifts a gum flap, may remove bone with a surgical handpiece, then sutures. Your role covers the safety checks beforehand, an aseptic set-up, suction and retraction during surgery, monitoring and reassuring the patient, clear aftercare advice and an accurate record.

items: Medical history updated and checked: anticoagulants, bisphosphonates, allergies, bleeding disorders.
Valid consent has been obtained by the dentist.
Confirm the correct tooth with the dentist, against the chart and treatment plan.
The correct, current radiograph is available.
Sterile instruments ready; open packs without touching the contents.

teach.h: The blood clot is the healing plug
teach.body: After extraction, a blood clot forms in the socket. It stops the bleeding and is the scaffold for healing. Biting on a gauze pack applies pressure that helps a stable clot form. Almost all post-op advice exists to protect that clot: no vigorous rinsing or spitting at first, nothing hot, no smoking or alcohol, no poking the socket. Give the advice verbally and in writing, and record that it was given.

items: Bite on the gauze for as long as the dentist advises.
Don't rinse or spit vigorously for the first 24 hours; after that, gentle warm salt-water rinses help.
Avoid hot drinks, alcohol, smoking and strenuous exercise for the rest of the day.
Expect some mild discomfort and swelling; take painkillers as advised.
If it bleeds, bite firmly on a clean, damp gauze pad. Contact the practice if bleeding doesn't stop.

teach.caption: Dry socket (alveolar osteitis) happens when the clot is lost or breaks down. Risks include smoking, difficult extractions and lower molars. The dentist usually irrigates and dresses the socket.

teach.text: Extracting the wrong tooth is a serious, avoidable patient safety incident. Never rely on memory: confirm the tooth with the dentist against the chart, treatment plan and the CORRECT radiograph before anything starts. And bleeding that won't stop is reported promptly, not left until the next day.

items: Pre-op: identity, medical history, consent, correct tooth, correct radiograph.
Forceps grasp the crown; elevators loosen teeth and remove roots and fragments.
Surgery: retract, suction, sterile saline irrigation, suture, count instruments.
Protect the clot: bite on gauze; no vigorous rinsing for 24 hours; no hot drinks, smoking or alcohol.
Persistent bleeding: report promptly. Worsening pain and bad taste after 2 to 4 days: dry socket, arrange review.

summary: You can now run the safety checks before an extraction, choose the right forceps and elevators, support a surgical extraction with suction, retraction and irrigation, give clear post-op advice that protects the clot, and recognise when a patient needs to be seen again.

A.q: An upper molar is to be removed under local anaesthetic. Which instrument grasps the crown to deliver the tooth?
A.why: Forceps grip the crown (or root) of the tooth to deliver it from the socket.

whyNot.0: Cryer's elevators remove roots, especially in lower molar sockets.
whyNot.2: A periosteal elevator lifts a gum flap off the bone.
whyNot.3: Warwick James elevators loosen teeth and roots; they don't grasp the crown.

A.q: A patient asks why they must bite on gauze after their extraction. What is the best explanation?
options: It numbs the socket for longer
Pressure helps a stable clot form
It keeps food out of the socket all day
A.why: Firm pressure on the socket helps bleeding stop and a stable blood clot form.

whyNot.3: The gauze is removed after a short time; its job is pressure, not a barrier.

A.q: Three days after an extraction, a patient phones with worsening throbbing pain and a bad taste. What is the best action?
options: Tell them this is normal healing
A.why: Worsening pain and a bad taste a few days after extraction suggest dry socket, which needs the dentist to see and treat it.

whyNot.0: Vigorous rinsing won't treat dry socket and can make things worse.
whyNot.1: Normal healing pain eases over time; it doesn't worsen.
whyNot.2: Delaying leaves the patient in severe pain without treatment.

B.q: A root fractures during an extraction and part of it remains in the socket. Which instrument is commonly used to remove it?
B.why: Elevators, such as Warwick James or Cryer's, are used to loosen and remove retained roots and fragments.

whyNot.1: Molar forceps grip a whole crown and can't reach a fragment in the socket.
whyNot.2: A Mitchell's trimmer can scrape or lift tissue but isn't the main tool for roots.
whyNot.3: A needle holder is for suturing.

B.q: Why should a patient avoid vigorous rinsing and spitting in the first 24 hours after an extraction?
options: It causes the socket to swell
It makes the anaesthetic wear off
It may dislodge the blood clot
B.why: Vigorous rinsing and spitting create suction and pressure that can wash out the clot, leading to bleeding or dry socket.

whyNot.0: Swelling is part of normal healing, not caused by rinsing.

B.q: Bone is being removed with a surgical handpiece. Why does the dentist ask for sterile saline?
options: To cool and irrigate the site
B.why: Sterile saline cools the bone to prevent heat damage and flushes debris from the surgical site.

whyNot.1: Gagging is managed by positioning and suction, not saline.

C.q: The extraction instruments are laid out and the patient is seated. Which check is most important for patient safety?
options: Confirm the tooth with the dentist
Ask whether they have eaten today
C.why: Confirming the correct tooth with the dentist, against the chart and radiograph, prevents a wrong-site extraction.

whyNot.1: Future bookings don't affect safety now.
whyNot.2: Having eaten may help prevent fainting, but it is far less critical than the right tooth.
whyNot.3: Comfort matters, but room temperature isn't a pre-op safety check.

C.q: The final suture has been placed after a surgical extraction. What should happen next?
options: Count the instruments, then tidy the field
Remove the sutures to check the socket
C.why: Counting instruments and sharps confirms nothing has been left behind and protects everyone from sharps injuries.

whyNot.0: The patient needs checking and post-op advice before leaving.
whyNot.2: Sutures are left in place to hold the tissues together.
whyNot.3: Vigorous rinsing could dislodge the clot.

C.q: A patient phones a few hours after an extraction. Which of these should be reported promptly to the dentist?
C.why: Persistent bleeding despite pressure needs prompt clinical advice and may need the patient to be seen.

whyNot.0: Mild tenderness is expected after an extraction.
whyNot.1: Some swelling is a normal response.
whyNot.3: Numbness wearing off is expected as the anaesthetic fades.

reteach.title: Think of a scab on a graze
reteach.question: If you keep picking a scab off a graze, what happens? How is that like a tooth socket?

blocks.body: When you graze your knee, a scab forms. It stops the bleeding and protects new skin growing underneath. Pick it, and it bleeds again and heals slowly. A tooth socket's blood clot is that scab, but it's in a wet, busy mouth, so it is easier to disturb. Hard rinsing, spitting, sucking on a cigarette, hot drinks and poking with the tongue all 'pick the scab'. If the clot is lost, the bone underneath is exposed and very painful: that's dry socket.

explain.body: Identity, updated medical history, consent, the correct tooth confirmed with the dentist, and the correct radiograph available. Open sterile packs without touching the contents.

explain.caption: 46 marked for extraction: check the chart, the plan and the radiograph all agree.

test.q: Before a surgical extraction, what should you confirm about radiographs?
options: That a new image is taken every visit
That the patient has seen the image
That the correct image is available
That the image is printed on paper
test.why: The dentist needs the correct, current radiograph of the right tooth to plan and carry out the extraction safely.

whyNot.0: Radiographs are only taken when justified, not routinely every visit.
whyNot.1: Showing the patient may help explain, but it isn't the safety check.
whyNot.3: Digital images on screen are fine; printing isn't required.

explain.body: Forceps grasp the crown. Upper forceps are roughly straight; lower forceps are at right angles. Elevators (Coupland's, Warwick James, Cryer's) loosen teeth and remove roots and fragments.

test.q: How can you tell lower extraction forceps from upper ones?
options: Beaks at right angles to handles
test.why: Lower forceps have beaks set at about 90° to the handles; upper forceps are roughly straight.

whyNot.2: Handle texture doesn't distinguish upper from lower.
whyNot.3: All extraction forceps have two beaks.

explain.body: Retract the flap and cheek with retractors, keep the field clear with suction, and irrigate with sterile saline while bone is removed. Sutures bring the tissue edges together. Count instruments after suturing.

items.label: Orange
items.sub: Infectious waste such as bloody swabs

test.q: During a surgical extraction, why is suction particularly important?
options: It reduces the need for anaesthetic
It keeps a clear field of view
test.why: Blood and saline quickly flood the site; suction keeps it clear so the dentist can see exactly what they are doing.

whyNot.0: Suction removes fluid; it doesn't sterilise anything.
whyNot.2: Suction doesn't affect how sutures dissolve.

explain.body: Bite on gauze; don't rinse vigorously for 24 hours; avoid hot drinks, smoking and alcohol. Expect mild discomfort and swelling. Report persistent bleeding promptly. Worsening pain and a bad taste after 2 to 4 days suggest dry socket. Record the treatment and advice given.

explain.caption: The tooth sits in a socket of alveolar bone, held by the periodontal ligament. After extraction, if the clot is lost, this bone is exposed: dry socket.

test.q: After a surgical extraction, which record entry is most important once the patient has left?
options: Only the time the patient arrived
The treatment carried out and advice given
The nurse's opinion of the patient
The cost of the instruments used
test.why: The clinical record must show exactly what was done and what post-op advice was given, for safety and legal reasons.

whyNot.0: Arrival time alone says nothing about the treatment or advice.
whyNot.2: Personal opinions don't belong in a clinical record; records must be factual.
whyNot.3: Instrument costs aren't part of the patient's clinical record.
